note: An MIT-professor pass: every line teaches the mechanism, never reads the on-screen caption. No digits, symbols or code names; every number is spoken in words.

lines: A sorted list of about a million numbers, stored plainly, takes a fixed amount of memory for every single one of them, no matter how those numbers happen to be spread out.
A counting argument says something sharper is possible: across every list of that size and range, no encoding can average fewer than a certain number of bits per entry — call it the honest floor.

Real schemes spend more than that floor, some by a little, some by a surprising amount. So here's the real question worth sitting with: whichever of them spends the fewest bits, is that also the one that decodes the fastest?
Here's a scheme built entirely around one small idea. Spend most of a byte on actual payload, and reserve just one bit of it to say whether another byte follows.

A small number fits in that payload with nothing left over, so it's written as a single byte. A larger number spills past what one byte's payload can hold, so a second byte gets chained on, flagged as a continuation of the first.
Here's something worth noticing about decoding this scheme, one byte at a time.
Before reading any of a particular number's bytes, does the decoder already know how many of them it's about to read — or does it only find that out byte by byte, as it goes?
answer: It only finds out byte by byte — there's no way to know in advance.

Each byte's own continuation flag has to actually be read before the decoder knows whether there's more coming, which makes every single one of those checks a genuine guess the processor has to make and might get wrong.

lines: Measure how many of those genuine guesses a real list of numbers actually forces, byte by byte, and the number lands just under two for every single entry decoded.

That's not a flaw in any particular implementation. It's the direct, unavoidable cost of a scheme whose very shape depends on the value being read — the processor simply cannot know ahead of time what's coming, so it has to guess, and sometimes it guesses wrong.
Here's a completely different way to spend those bits. Instead of deciding one byte at a time, break the whole list into fixed-size groups first.
For each group, find the widest number it contains, and give every single entry in that group exactly that many bits — not one bit more, and critically, not one flag bit, for any of them.
Nothing inside the group needs deciding anymore. The width was settled once, for the whole group, before a single value gets unpacked.
Suppose a group of entries is almost entirely small and tidy — except for one number that happens to be much larger than all the rest.
That group still has to settle on exactly one width for every entry inside it. So what happens to that width?
answer: It widens to cover the one large number — and every other entry in that same group now pays for a width none of them actually needed.
A group's width is set by its single largest member, full stop. One outlier doesn't just cost itself extra bits; it drags every ordinary neighbor sharing its group along with it.

lines: So here's the fix, and it's a small one. Choose a width that comfortably covers most of a group's entries, and simply set the rare oversized ones aside in their own separate list.
Decode the group at that narrow, comfortable width, then go back and patch each set-aside value into its rightful place afterward.
Measured against a group that had to widen for its outliers, this costs dramatically less — and it still never needs a single per-entry flag while decoding the group itself.

Back to the byte-at-a-time scheme for a moment, with one change. Instead of one flag bit living inside every single byte, pull four numbers together and describe all four of their lengths with a single shared byte, set just ahead of them.
Now decoding only has to consult one of these shared bytes for every four numbers, instead of checking a flag inside every single byte along the way.

A later version of this same grouped idea takes one more step: instead of weaving those shared length-bytes in among the actual numbers, it pulls every single one of them out into its own stream entirely, read just ahead of all the data.
Does moving them out like that change how many bits the whole encoding spends?
answer: No — it's the exact same number of bits. Only where they sit changes, not how many there are.

What that separation buys isn't a smaller encoding at all — it's a data portion that now sits together as one uninterrupted run, which is exactly the shape a wide, single-instruction read wants to work with.

lines: Now put the two measurements side by side for every scheme covered so far: how many bits each one spends, and how many genuine guesses its decoder has to make.

Here's the twist: those two rankings don't agree with each other. The fixed-width group scheme, on this particular list, actually spends more bits than the simple byte-at-a-time one did — yet it asks its decoder to make almost no guesses at all.
Patch away that scheme's rare outliers, and it keeps that same tiny guess count while taking back nearly everything the extra bits had cost.
This same family of ideas shows up directly inside real systems that have to decode enormous lists, fast, over and over.
One well-known search engine's own list format decodes fixed groups at a time, patching away outliers in one kind of group but not another, depending on what each group is actually used for.
A widely used columnar file format names its own two separate schemes for exactly this job — one built on the group-and-patch idea, another on run-length grouping instead.
So here's the lesson this whole topic was really building toward: the fastest way to decode something was never about finding the smallest encoding of it.
It was about removing the decisions a value's own content could otherwise force the decoder to make, one guess at a time.
And the plain sorted list from the previous lesson — the one container that simply stored its values as they were — turns out to have been exactly this scheme's own starting point the entire time.
